summary: Maps NETCONF onto the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP), a framework for building application protocols. It specifies how NETCONF sessions and messages are carried over a BEEP channel. This RFC is historic.

eli5.summary: NETCONF is a way to send settings to network machines. This note describes carrying those messages on a delivery service called BEEP. Hardly anyone used it, so it is now historic.

questions: what port does netconf over beep use
is netconf over beep still used
subtitle: How to carry NETCONF network-management sessions over BEEP, and why it is now Historic.

tldr.problem: NETCONF is designed to run over several application protocols, so it needs a defined mapping onto each one it can use.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC maps NETCONF onto BEEP on TCP port 831, using TLS and SASL for security, a dedicated NETCONF profile on a BEEP channel, and BEEP messages to carry hello, rpc and rpc-reply.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4744 is now Historic and has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4744 is Historic and has been updated by RFC 8996. It describes a NETCONF transport mapping that is no longer a current standard.

sections.title: Why BEEP for NETCONF
sections.content:
The NETCONF protocol of RFC 4741 is a simple way to manage a network device and is meant to work over several application protocols. This RFC specifies the mapping onto the Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol (BEEP), defined in RFC 3080.

The RFC gives these reasons. BEEP is a natural fit for transporting XML. It is peer-to-peer, so either the manager or the agent can start the connection. That helps with large numbers of intermittently connected devices and with devices that must reverse the management connection because of firewalls and NATs. BEEP also uses SASL and TLS, which give a direct mapping to the existing command line interface (CLI) security model and strong encryption.

In this document a manager is a NETCONF client and an agent is a NETCONF server. The words client and server are avoided because BEEP is peer-to-peer.
sections.eli5: BEEP lets either side start the conversation. That is handy when a router is behind a locked door and has to call out to the manager instead.

sections.title: Session Establishment
sections.content:
Managers and agents may each be BEEP listeners or initiators. The initiator connects to the listener on TCP port 831. After the greetings, both sides SHOULD announce support for TLS and optionally SASL. If TLS is used, the listener starts a channel with the TLS profile, and a new greeting is sent by both sides afterwards.

After all greetings, the agent MUST advertise the NETCONF profile and the manager MUST NOT. An agent side that receives a greeting containing the NETCONF profile MUST close the connection, and if neither side offers it, the listener MUST close the connection.

If SASL is wanted, the initiator then opens a channel only to authenticate, and closes it on completion. The SASL PLAIN mechanism MUST NOT be used over unencrypted channels, and when used with TLS it MUST NOT be advertised in the first greeting, only in the one after TLS negotiation succeeds.
sections.eli5: First the two sides say hello and agree on a secret tunnel. Then only the device being managed says it speaks NETCONF, so both know who is who.

sections.title: Channels, Operations and Teardown
sections.content:
The manager opens a new BEEP channel and names the single NETCONF profile, http://iana.org/beep/netconf. NETCONF messages are sent with a Content-type of text/xml. The two sides then swap NETCONF <hello> elements on that channel to learn each other's capabilities.

Nearly all operations use the <rpc> element. The manager sends the request in a BEEP MSG and the agent answers with BEEP RPY messages on the same channel. Either may be split across several BEEP frames.

On <close-session> from the manager, once the agent has finished all RPCs, it closes BEEP channel 0. The agent can also start a close this way, and should allow a reasonable period for a manager to release a lock first. Closing channel 0 releases all locks. After a BEEP close or after sending <close-session>, a manager MUST NOT send further requests.
sections.eli5: The manager opens a special lane just for NETCONF, they swap lists of what each can do, and then the manager sends commands and gets answers back on the same lane. To finish, the lanes are closed in order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Configuration data often contains passwords, user names, service descriptions and topology, so sending it in the clear leaves devices open to person-in-the-middle attacks. A NETCONF transport must at least support confidentiality and authentication. Here, TLS provides confidentiality and the server certificate authenticates the server. The client MUST be ready to validate a server certificate and SHOULD reject invalid ones by default.

The RFC warns about circular dependencies in validation: an OCSP server may be unreachable at network cold-start, so a core router should not depend on one to receive its configuration. A client may offer a certificate during TLS. Authorization can be based on subject name or certificate authority.

If the client did not authenticate through TLS, the server SHOULD advertise SASL profiles. Implementations MUST support DIGEST-MD5 and MAY support others such as the One-Time Password mechanism. The minimum may be PLAIN only when TLS is established. No authorization model is specified; an rpc-error with "permission denied" is sufficient.
sections.eli5: Settings for a router can include secret passwords, so the tunnel must be locked and each side must prove who it is before anything is sent.
